Subject: Post-call: Tool/Function Calling integration patterns & next steps

Alex / Samira 1 thanks again for the time today. Quick recap + recommended next steps from our discovery: 

Recap:
- Goal: add tool/function calling to FinApps workflows for automated data fetches (account balances, transaction lookups) and to enable deterministic actions (create support tickets, trigger payouts).
- Constraints: must run inside FinApps VPC for production (private deployment), RBAC + audit logs required, and low-99 latency target (~200ms for critical lookups).
- Current infra: microservices behind API gateway, auth via short-lived service tokens, existing embeddings index for search.

Recommended integration approach (high-level):
1) SDK & auth:
   - Use Redwood SDK client in your backend (service account + short-lived signing tokens for Private). For hosted POC you can start with an API key scoped to dev env.
   - Key rotation: recommend service-account + short-lived JWTs with KMS integration for production.

2) Tool/function calling patterns (what we discussed):
   - Tool definitions: expose each backend action as a typed function (name, input schema, outputs). Keep signatures explicit (JSON Schema) so the LLM emits structured arguments.
   - Tool choice: prefer small, single-purpose tools (e.g., get_account_balance(account_id), fetch_transactions(account_id, start, end), create_support_ticket(payload)). Avoid monolithic tool surfaces.
   - Parallel tools: for independent lookups (balances for multiple accounts, or fetching enrichment from third-party services) call tools in parallel and aggregate results. This reduces tail latency.
   - Error handling: define per-tool retry budgets and timeouts; on partial failures aggregate successes and mark failures in the response. Provide fallbacks: 1) cached value 2) degrade to LLM-only summary with a clear provenance flag.

3) Routing & model selection:
   - Smart routing: route control-plane / orchestration calls to a lower-cost model for non-latency-critical tasks (e.g., summarization), and route critical function-calling to a verified low-latency model instance.
   - Fallbacks: automatic fallback to a compatible model variant when capacity constrained.

4) Structured output & rerankers:
   - Emit JSON for tool arguments and for final structured responses. Use a strict schema to validate outputs before invoking tools.
   - For retrieval workflows, use embeddings for candidate fetch then a lightweight reranker model (or LLM with a rank prompt) to pick top-K. Keep reranker close to the runtime to avoid cross-region hops.

Action items / next steps:
- I attached a short "redwood-tool-calling-reference.pdf" with example function signatures and an example SDK snippet.
- I also attached a sample dockerized config (demo-sample-config.yaml) for your eng team to spin up a POC.
- Proposed next call: technical deep dive with engineering \u2014 can we do Mon 3/15 or Tue 3/16 10am PT?

If helpful I can include a minimal end-to-end demo repo showing: SDK init, token exchange, tool definitions, parallel invocation pattern, and reranker pipeline.

Alex \u2014 great questions, answers inline below. Also pasted a short SDK example at the bottom for quick reference.

1) Okta short-lived tokens & rotation:
   - Yes. For Redwood Private we integrate with customer IdP to mint short-lived tokens. Pattern: your backend exchanges a Okta-signed assertion -> Redwood issues a short-lived service token scoped to the deployment. We support automated rotation via your KMS/HSM. We can share our IAM integration checklist for your security team.

2) Partial failures & parallel tool strategy:
   - Best practice: mark each tool call with a correlation id and a per-tool timeout. Execute independent tool calls in parallel with a scatter-gather pattern.
   - Aggregation strategy: return successes immediately in the response payload and include a structured "errors" array listing failed tools with error codes and timestamps. That lets the UX show partial results and surface specific retry buttons.
   - Fallback hierarchy: cache -> retry (with backoff) -> LLM-based approximation (only if acceptable). We recommend you define SLOs for each tool to decide when to surface approximations.

3) SDK snippets (JS):
   - Example (pseudo):
     const client = new RedwoodClient({ baseUrl: process.env.REDWOOD_URL, token: await getShortLivedToken() });
     // Define a tool signature so the model can call it
     const tools = [{ name: 'get_account_balance', input_schema: { account_id: 'string' }, timeout_ms: 250 }];
     const resp = await client.callModel({ model: 'redwood-lowlatency-v1', prompt, tools, parallel: true });

   - Python would mirror the same concepts. I attached a full runnable sample in the Drive link.

Additional notes on validation & structured output:
- Validate the LLM-produced JSON against the declared schema before invoking the tool. If validation fails, either ask the model for a corrected payload or use a best-effort sanitizer.

Monitoring & observability:
- We emit per-tool metrics (latency, success_rate), per-request cost breakdown, and a correlation id you can pass through logs. We'll also instrument SLO-based alerts for error-rate spikes.

Looping in a couple engineering notes before the deep dive:
- Routing/quantization: for heavy embedding workloads we suggest quantized model variants on dedicated hosts and routing those requests to Dedicated pool to control cost/throughput.
- Reranker placement: keep ranker in the same region as embeddings storage to avoid cross-region network tail.
- For parallel calls, instrument a short-circuit for cascading failures (e.g., >50% of vendor tools failing -> open circuit to prevent user-visible timeouts).

I'll demo a sample parallel-invoke test harness in the deep-dive.
